title: White Fang
author: Jack London
setting: The Mackenzie and Yukon country of the Canadian North in the 1890s, then the Santa Clara Valley in California
lengthNote: Five parts and twenty-five chapters, about 72,000 words — more than twice the length of The Call of the Wild
openingLine: Dark spruce forest frowned on either side the frozen waterway.
summary: A wolf cub, three-quarters wolf and a quarter dog, is born in a cave on the Mackenzie and taken into an Indian camp as a yearling. London then hands him from master to master — a hunter who beats him, a coward who makes him fight for money, a mining engineer who decides to love him — and records what each pressure does to his temperament. The book was written as the deliberate reverse of The Call of the Wild, and its argument is stated outright: the animal is clay, and the world moulds it. What makes the novel more than a thesis is that the moulding is shown from the inside, in a creature who cannot name what is happening to him.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of White Fang
sourceText.note: The novel is divided into five parts, each with chapters numbered afresh from I; references give both, as Part III, Chapter 2.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Six monthly instalments in Outing from May, then the Macmillan book in October, with colour plates by Charles Livingston Bull.

atAGlance.label: Companion
atAGlance.note: London planned it as the earlier book run backwards: not a dog going wild but a wolf coming in to the fire.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The title character is not born until Part II, and does not meet a kind human until the last chapter of Part IV.

atAGlance.label: The argument
atAGlance.note: The word 'clay' is applied in turn to White Fang, to Beauty Smith and to an escaped convict: nobody in the book made himself.

structure.label: Part I
structure.title: The Wild: two men, a coffin and a hungry pack
structure.summary: Henry and Bill haul a dead lord's coffin down a frozen river while a famished wolf pack, led by a reddish she-wolf, picks off their dogs one night at a time. Bill is killed trying to save a dog; Henry is saved by a relief party with hours to spare. The wolf cub of the title has not yet been born, and the part is a prologue about what the Wild does to anything that moves.

scenes.title: The Trail of the Meat
scenes.summary: Six dogs are fed and seven come to eat; by morning there are five.

scenes.title: The She-Wolf
scenes.summary: The dogs are lured away one by one by a wolf with a dog's ways; Bill has three cartridges left.

scenes.title: The Hunger Cry
scenes.summary: Bill goes after the pack and does not come back; Henry sits inside a ring of fire until men arrive.

structure.label: Part II
structure.title: Born of the Wild: the lair and the law of meat
structure.summary: The she-wolf, half dog herself, is won by the old wolf One Eye and litters in a cave by a frozen stream. One grey cub outlives his brothers and sisters, learns that the cave mouth is a wall of light, breaks through it, kills ptarmigan chicks and is very nearly killed by a weasel and a lynx. The cub does not have a name yet; London calls him the grey cub and shows the world being sorted, by trial, into what hurts and what does not.

scenes.title: The Battle of the Fangs
scenes.summary: The pack finds meat and breaks up; three males fight over the she-wolf and One Eye wins.

scenes.title: The Lair
scenes.summary: One Eye hunts through a famine for his mate's litter and takes a lynx's kill.

scenes.title: The Grey Cub
scenes.summary: The fiercest of five cubs learns hurt from his mother's paw and survives the famine that kills the others.

scenes.title: The Wall of the World
scenes.summary: He walks into the wall of light, falls down the slope, and finds the world made of things to eat.

scenes.title: The Law of Meat
scenes.summary: His mother kills the lynx that killed One Eye; the cub learns that life lives on life.

structure.label: Part III
structure.title: The gods of the fire: Grey Beaver's camp
structure.summary: Indians on the Mackenzie recognise the she-wolf as Kiche, a dog who ran away in a famine, and name her cub White Fang. He is tied, beaten, and set upon by Lip-lip and the whole puppy pack until he becomes the most hated and most efficient fighter in the camp. When Grey Beaver's people move on he tries the Wild for one night and comes back of his own accord. By the end of the part he is a sled leader in a covenant with a god he serves without loving.

scenes.title: The Makers of Fire
scenes.summary: The cub bites a man's hand, is named, and burns his nose on the first fire he sees.

scenes.title: The Bondage
scenes.summary: Kiche is sold away up the Mackenzie; Lip-lip begins the persecution that shapes White Fang's temper.

scenes.title: The Outcast
scenes.summary: He learns to fight a pack and to kill a single dog quickly, and the camp learns to hate him.

scenes.title: The Trail of the Gods
scenes.summary: Left behind when the camp moves, he spends a night in the Wild and runs back to the fire.

scenes.title: The Covenant
scenes.summary: Harnessed to Mit-sah's puppy sled, he takes revenge on Lip-lip and becomes a working animal.

scenes.title: The Famine
scenes.summary: A great hunger drives him back to the woods; he meets Kiche, kills Lip-lip, and returns when the fish come.

structure.label: Part IV
structure.title: The superior gods: Fort Yukon, Beauty Smith and Weedon Scott
structure.summary: In the gold-rush summer of 1898 Grey Beaver trades at Fort Yukon, loses everything to whisky, and sells White Fang to Beauty Smith, a coward who keeps him chained, laughs at him and fights him for money as the Fighting Wolf. A bulldog named Cherokee is choking him to death in the ring when a mining engineer, Weedon Scott, beats Smith off, buys the wolf and, against every warning, sets out to undo what men have done to him. The part ends with the word love, and with White Fang breaking a window to follow the steamboat south.

scenes.title: The Enemy of His Kind
scenes.summary: White Fang leads Grey Beaver's sled, hates all dogs, and meets the white gods at Fort Yukon.

scenes.title: The Mad God
scenes.summary: Beauty Smith buys him with whisky; three times he goes back to Grey Beaver and is beaten.

scenes.title: The Reign of Hate
scenes.summary: He is exhibited in a cage, then matched against dogs, wolves and a lynx in the ring.

scenes.title: The Clinging Death
scenes.summary: Cherokee the bulldog takes his throat; Weedon Scott and Matt break the grip and take him.

scenes.title: The Indomitable
scenes.summary: He bites Scott, is not clubbed, and is stroked instead — and does not know what to do about it.

scenes.title: The Love-Master
scenes.summary: Like becomes love; Scott goes away and White Fang stops eating; he learns to snuggle.

structure.label: Part V
structure.title: The Southland: Sierra Vista and the sleeping wolf
structure.summary: Scott takes him to his father's estate in the Santa Clara Valley, where a new set of laws has to be learned: chickens are not meat, dogs that bark are not to be killed, and the sheepdog Collie may bully him with impunity. He saves the master from a runaway horse and wins the household. When Jim Hall, a convict Judge Scott once sentenced, breaks into the house at night, White Fang kills him and is nearly killed himself. He recovers, is named the Blessed Wolf, and walks out into the sun to be climbed on by Collie's puppies.

scenes.title: The Long Trail
scenes.summary: Scott packs the grip that means departure; White Fang howls, then breaks a window and is on the boat.

scenes.title: The Southland
scenes.summary: San Francisco, a baggage car, a carriage and a sheepdog who will not let him pass.

scenes.title: The God's Domain
scenes.summary: He learns the laws of a house with many gods, and that a cuff from the master hurts more than a club.

scenes.title: The Call of Kind
scenes.summary: He runs with Collie in the woods as Kiche and One Eye once ran, and the master rides alone.

scenes.title: The Sleeping Wolf
scenes.summary: Jim Hall comes up the stairs in the dark; a wolf with three bullets in him is called Blessed.

characters.name: White Fang
characters.role: A cub of the Wild, three parts wolf and one part dog
characters.summary: Fiercer than his litter-mates from birth, and the only one to survive the cave. Everything after that is treatment: the puppy pack makes him a fighter, Grey Beaver's club makes him obedient, Beauty Smith makes him a fiend, and Weedon Scott's hand makes him capable of love. London insists at every stage that he does not reason any of this out, which is what keeps him an animal and not an allegory.
characters.clue: Named for the colour of his teeth by the man who first tied him to a stick, this one is exhibited in a cage for fifty cents a look, nearly strangled by a bulldog, and ends up licking a puppy's face on a lawn in California.

characters.name: Kiche, the she-wolf
characters.role: White Fang's mother; a wolf-dog cross who ran from the camp in a famine
characters.summary: She leads the starving pack in Part I with a trick no true wolf could manage — she walks up to the dogs at feeding time and lures them out to be eaten. The book then reveals that the trick is her dog's blood. She is the fiercest thing in the lair and the first thing White Fang learns to fear; when Grey Beaver's man calls her name she crawls to him, and the cub learns from her what submission looks like.
characters.clue: Red-furred and half tame, she draws sled dogs out of camp to their deaths, litters in a cave, and crawls on her belly to the first man who says her name.

relationships.label: returns to and is sold by

characters.name: One Eye
characters.role: An old grey wolf, White Fang's father
characters.summary: He wins the she-wolf by letting two younger rivals wear each other down and then closing on the survivor with his one good side. London gives him the most sustained hunting sequence in the book — the porcupine, the lynx, the ptarmigan he drops and remembers — and then kills him offstage in a fight with the lynx, so that the cub grows up fatherless without ever being told so.
characters.clue: Scarred, grizzled and blind on the left side, he runs always at his mate's right, waits out a fight between two younger wolves, and dies to a lynx while his cubs are still in the cave.

characters.name: Henry and Bill
characters.role: Two men hauling a coffin down a frozen river
characters.summary: They exist to show the reader what the pack can do before the pack has a point of view. Bill counts the fish and the dogs and cannot make the numbers agree; Henry is the steadier man and the one who lives. Their talk is the only extended human dialogue in the first two parts, and London uses it to establish the price of everything in the North, including a lord's funeral.
characters.clue: Two men on a trail with three cartridges, six dogs and a dead lord in a box, arguing about why seven animals came to be fed.

characters.name: Grey Beaver
characters.role: A Mackenzie Indian, White Fang's first master
characters.summary: He names the cub, ties him to a stick, beats him when he bites, and is entirely just by his own lights: he gives meat and hurt in proportion and expects work. London is careful not to make him cruel — his failing is that he has no affection to give, so the dog he shapes is faithful without being fond. Whisky at Fort Yukon undoes him in a few weeks, and he sells White Fang to pay for more.
characters.clue: He decides a cub's name by the colour of its teeth, rules by stick and by meat, and trades his best dog for bottles at a Yukon fort.

characters.name: Lip-lip
characters.role: The bully of the puppy pack in Grey Beaver's camp
characters.summary: Older and heavier than White Fang, he picks him out on the first day and never lets up, and the narrator later says plainly that without Lip-lip White Fang would have grown up more like a dog. He is the first instance of the book's rule that temperament is made by what is done to you. White Fang kills him in a single rush during the famine, without ceremony.
characters.clue: The camp's biggest puppy, who chooses one newcomer for his special object of persecution and is killed by him in the woods years later in the time of hunger.

characters.name: Beauty Smith
characters.role: The cook at Fort Yukon who buys White Fang to fight him
characters.summary: Ugly, cringing and vicious, and the only human being the narrator explains at the same length as the wolf. London refuses to call him responsible: his clay was moulded too. He owns White Fang for less than a year and does more damage in that time than the Wild managed in three, because he has discovered that the animal can be driven mad by laughter.
characters.clue: A snivelling cook with a jaw like a shelf who laughs at a chained wolf until it goes mad, and charges gold dust for the sight of it.

characters.name: Weedon Scott
characters.role: A mining engineer who buys White Fang out of the fighting ring
characters.summary: He arrives in Part IV, Chapter 4 and hits Beauty Smith in the face before he has said a word. His project — to pay back what mankind owes one animal — is described as a matter of principle, and the book keeps count of what it costs him: a bitten hand, a slaughtered chicken run, a dog that stops eating when he leaves. He is the fourth god in White Fang's life and the first who does not use the club.
characters.clue: An engineer who breaks up a dog fight with his fists, buys the loser for a hundred and fifty dollars, and teaches it what a hand is for.

characters.name: Collie
characters.summary: She meets White Fang at the carriage step and refuses to let a wolf into the house, and for months afterwards she uses the licence of her sex to punish him while he is forbidden to answer. The book treats her as the last law he has to learn: that there is such a thing as a grievance he may not settle by force. When she finally runs off into the woods with him, the narrator matches it to Kiche and One Eye running in the Northland.
characters.clue: A sheepdog with an ancestral grudge against wolves who blocks the drive, nips the newcomer for a season, and finally leads him into the woods.

characters.name: Jim Hall
characters.role: An escaped convict from San Quentin
characters.summary: He appears for a few pages at the end and is given the book's argument in miniature: a slum boy made into a beast by prison, wrongly convicted once, and now hunting the judge who sentenced him. London calls him a monstrosity in the same words he used for Beauty Smith. He never speaks; White Fang meets him on the stairs in the dark.
characters.clue: A man the narrator calls soft clay in the hands of society, who climbs a staircase at night towards a sleeping judge and meets something waiting at the top.

themes.name: Nature and nurture
themes.summary: London states the thesis in a figure he repeats until it becomes structural: the animal is clay, and environment is the hand. What makes the book more than a lecture is that the figure is applied evenly — to the wolf, to the coward who torments him and to the convict who dies on the stairs — so that nobody in the novel is allowed to be simply good or simply wicked by birth.
themes.development: The cub is sorted by hurt in Part II; Lip-lip and the club shape him in Part III; Beauty Smith makes a fiend in Part IV; and Weedon Scott's project in the same part is described as a reflux of being, a re-moulding attempted after the clay has hardened.

themes.name: The Wild and the law of meat
themes.summary: The Northland in this book is an agent with intentions: it wants movement to stop, and it laughs. Against it stands one rule, which the cub learns without ever thinking it — eat or be eaten. London calls this law rather than cruelty, and the distinction is the same one he had drawn in The Call of the Wild, now seen from the wolf's side of the fire.
themes.development: Part I shows the Wild consuming men; Part II gives it a philosophy in the cub's education; from Part III onward it is what White Fang carries inside him into camps and houses, and the last part keeps saying the wolf in him only sleeps.

themes.name: Gods, masters and the covenant
themes.summary: The Indians are gods to White Fang because they make fire and hurl clubs, and London works out the theology carefully: gods punish, gods give meat, gods may not be bitten. Service is the price of the fire, and the novel distinguishes three kinds of it — the duty and awe owed to Grey Beaver, the terror owed to Beauty Smith, and the love that Scott alone is paid.
themes.development: The cub gives the man-animals the trail as their right in Part III; the covenant between dog and man is named in the sled chapter; the white men at Fort Yukon are superior gods again; and Sierra Vista in Part V is a domain with many gods and a more complicated law.

themes.name: The outcast
themes.summary: White Fang is set apart three times over: from the wolves by the fire, from the dogs by his wolf blood, and from the puppy pack by Lip-lip's choice of him. London makes solitude the engine of ferocity. He is dangerous because he has never played, and the book measures every later kindness against a creature who has no idea what to do with company.
themes.development: Chapter 3 of Part III is called The Outcast; the reign of hate in Part IV is enforced by a cage that keeps a crowd at exactly the right distance; and the last chapters show him learning, with visible difficulty, to be climbed on by puppies.

themes.name: Love as redemption
themes.summary: Love enters the novel late and is treated as a physical process — a potency touched to life, an evolution of like into something stronger — rather than a sentiment. London is unsentimental about its mechanics: it begins with a hand that does not strike, it is confirmed by a departure that makes the animal stop eating, and it expresses itself in snuggling, which the narrator calls the final word.
themes.development: Absent from the first three parts, named at the end of Part IV, and tested in Part V by a house full of people, a horse that bolts and a man on the stairs.

themes.name: Power, and the cruelty of cowards
themes.summary: The narrator observes that all life likes power and then shows what it looks like in someone who has very little: Beauty Smith, beaten by every man he meets, takes it out on a chained wolf. The book is unusually direct about how cruelty is manufactured, and it draws the same line under Jim Hall, made into a beast by straitjackets and clubbings. The Wild's power is at least impersonal; man's is not.
themes.development: Grey Beaver's club is power used as law; Beauty Smith's laughter is power used for pleasure; Scott's refusal to club a dog that has just bitten him is the book's first demonstration of power withheld.

techniques.name: The animal point of view
techniques.definition: Narration tied to the perceptions of a creature that cannot use language, so that thought has to be shown as sensation, memory and behaviour.
techniques.inThisBook: The cave mouth is a wall of light, men are man-animals and then gods, and the narrator keeps marking the limit — he did not formulate the law, he merely lived it — so that the reader has the concept and the wolf has only the experience.

techniques.name: Grand diction for animal experience
techniques.definition: Deliberately heightened, Latinate vocabulary applied to creatures and events that would ordinarily be described plainly.
techniques.inThisBook: A cub leaving a cave is compared to the first man landing on Mars; a dog's temper is described as an adamantine texture; a puppy's fear is a matter of generalisations upon the world. The gap between the grand phrase and the small event is where London's comedy and his seriousness both live.

techniques.name: Clay: the returning figure
techniques.definition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.inThisBook: The clay of him was so moulded — said of White Fang in Part IV, then of Beauty Smith, and finally of Jim Hall, a slum child described as soft clay in the hands of society. Each return widens the thesis from one animal to everyone.

techniques.name: The Wild as antagonist
techniques.definition: Place and weather made to press on the people living in them, rather than to decorate the scene.
techniques.inThisBook: The opening pages give the frozen land a personality — it frowns, it laughs, it aims to destroy movement — before a single character is introduced, and the ring of eyes around the fire in Part I is the Wild made visible.

techniques.name: The intruding narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator who steps forward to generalise, moralise or admit uncertainty.
techniques.inThisBook: London interrupts constantly to explain what his animal cannot: that it is easier to lean on another than to stand alone, that all life likes power, that the blame for Beauty Smith lay elsewhere. The intrusions are the novel's argument, and they are the part modern readers most often resist.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: The three masters are a controlled experiment in treatment — Grey Beaver's justice, Beauty Smith's cruelty, Weedon Scott's kindness — applied to one animal in sequence, and the Southland sheepdog Collie is set against Kiche as the mate at the other end of the journey.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs.
techniques.inThisBook: Henry and Bill's trail talk and Matt the dog-musher's Klondike speech are respelled — feedin', wisht, ben licked — and set against a narrator with the whole vocabulary of evolutionary science, which is the book's own version of the gap between the fire and the Wild.

quotations.text: It is not the way of the Wild to like movement. Life is an offence to it, for life is movement; and the Wild aims always to destroy movement.
quotations.context: The third paragraph of the novel, as two men haul a coffin along a frozen river.
quotations.analysis: The Wild is given a will and a dislike before it is given a single wolf, and the sentence works by definition rather than description: life is movement, therefore the land that freezes water is at war with life. The capital W makes it a proper noun, and the book will keep it as a character throughout.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter 1

quotations.text: It was the masterful and incommunicable wisdom of eternity laughing at the futility of life and the effort of life. It was the Wild, the savage, frozen-hearted Northland Wild.
quotations.context: The opening paragraph, describing the silence of the frozen land.
quotations.analysis: Two sentences that start with the same two words, the first enormous and abstract, the second a name. The laughter belongs to the land, not to any creature in it, and the phrase 'the effort of life' quietly announces that the book's subject will be effort — hauling, hunting, learning — against an audience that finds it funny.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter 1

quotations.text: And this was the epitaph of a dead dog on the Northland trail⁠—less scant than the epitaph of many another dog, of many a man.
quotations.context: The chapter's last sentence, after Bill and Henry agree that Fatty was always a fool dog.
quotations.analysis: The epitaph is two men's dismissive remarks over breakfast, and the narrator grades it as generous. The closing turn from dog to man is the first time the book puts the two species on one scale, and it does so through what each is worth when dead — a lord in a coffin has just been discussed on the same terms.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter 1

quotations.text: So to him the entrance of the cave was a wall⁠—a wall of light. As the sun was to the outside dweller, this wall was to him the sun of his world. It attracted him as a candle attracts a moth.
quotations.context: The grey cub, still in the lair, before he has learned what an entrance is.
quotations.analysis: London builds the cub's world out of what it lacks: no concept of passage, so the opening must be a wall. The moth simile is the first hint of danger in a paragraph about attraction, and the chapter that follows is titled after the wall, because breaking through it is the cub's first act of will.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter 3

quotations.text: Thus he learned hurt; and on top of it he learned to avoid hurt, first, by not incurring the risk of it; and second, when he had incurred the risk, by dodging and by retreating. These were conscious actions, and were the results of his first generalisations upon the world.
quotations.context: The cub's mother rebukes his crawling towards the light with her nose and paw.
quotations.analysis: The first lesson is dealt by the mother, not the Wild, which is the book's argument in miniature: hurt comes from those closest. 'Generalisations upon the world' is philosopher's language for a puppy learning to flinch, and the numbered clauses — first, second — turn a reflex into a curriculum.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter 3

quotations.text: The cub had broken through the wall of the world, the unknown had let go its hold of him, and here he was without hurt. But the first man on Mars would have experienced less unfamiliarity than did he.
quotations.context: The cub walks into the light and out of the cave for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The wall of light has become the wall of the world, and the fear that guarded it is personified as a hand letting go. Then the scale jumps to Mars: London reaches for the largest available image of first contact and gives it to a creature the size of a loaf. The comedy is deliberate and so is the seriousness.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter 4

quotations.text: Life lived on life. There were the eaters and the eaten. The law was: eat or be eaten. He did not formulate the law in clear, set terms and moralise about it. He did not even think the law; he merely lived the law without thinking about it at all.
quotations.context: The cub has begun to follow his mother on the meat-trail.
quotations.analysis: Five sentences that shrink as they go, from a general truth to a three-word law to a description of not thinking. The narrator states the rule and immediately withdraws it from the cub, so that the reader holds a philosophy the animal only performs — the book's characteristic division of labour.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter 5

quotations.text: Wherefore is there in him little dog and much wolf. His fangs be white, and White Fang shall be his name. I have spoken.
quotations.speaker: Grey Beaver
quotations.context: Grey Beaver, having recognised the she-wolf as Kiche, works out the cub's parentage and names him.
quotations.analysis: The name is a reckoning of blood — one part dog, three parts wolf — followed by a physical fact, and it is conferred by the first human who owns him. The formal cadence of the speech ('Wherefore', 'I have spoken') is London's convention for Indian dialogue, and it makes the naming a legal act rather than an endearment.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter 1

quotations.text: In fashion distantly resembling the way men look upon the gods they create, so looked White Fang upon the man-animals before him. They were superior creatures, of a verity, gods.
quotations.context: The cub watches the Indians move about their camp on the first day of his captivity.
quotations.analysis: Note the direction of the comparison: men create gods, and the wolf's awe is said to resemble that. London is a sceptic writing a religious experience from the outside, and the phrase 'the gods they create' tells the reader that the Indians' divinity is a product of the observer — which is exactly what the novel will show when White Fang later meets white men and promotes them above his old masters.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter 1

quotations.text: It was a placing of his destiny in another’s hands, a shifting of the responsibilities of existence. This in itself was compensation, for it is always easier to lean upon another than to stand alone.
quotations.context: White Fang begins to yield to the rule of the man-animals.
quotations.analysis: The submission of a wolf to a camp is rewritten as a general truth about anybody, in the present tense and with 'always'. The narrator's generalisations are the most argued-over feature of the book, and this one is doing something subtle: it makes domestication a relief rather than a defeat, and quietly implicates the reader.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter 2

quotations.text: Insidiously, and by remote ways, as well as by the power of stick and stone and clout of hand, were the shackles of White Fang’s bondage being riveted upon him.
quotations.context: The narrator sums up how camp life is working on the cub.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is inverted so that the shackles arrive last, after a long run of means, and the vocabulary — bondage, riveted, shackles — is that of slavery rather than pet-keeping. London wants the reader to feel the cost of the fire even while the cub is coming to like it, and the two adverbs 'insidiously' and 'remote' suggest the kindnesses are the more effective chains.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter 2

quotations.text: The possession of a god implies service. White Fang’s was a service of duty and awe, but not of love. He did not know what love was.
quotations.context: Grey Beaver has made White Fang lead dog of the sled team.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences that get shorter and plainer, ending on a flat statement of ignorance. The chapter is called The Covenant, and this is its small print: the first covenant is a labour contract. The word love is withheld here so that it can arrive, an entire part later, as a discovery rather than a given.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter 5

quotations.text: Thus, had White Fang never come in to the fires of man, the Wild would have moulded him into a true wolf. But the gods had given him a different environment, and he was moulded into a dog that was rather wolfish, but that was a dog and not a wolf.
quotations.context: White Fang returns to the camp of his own accord at the end of the famine.
quotations.analysis: The verb 'moulded' is used twice in two sentences, once for the Wild and once for the gods, to insist that both are the same kind of force acting on the same material. The definition of what he has become is deliberately fussy — 'rather wolfish, but ... a dog' — because the book will spend two more parts arguing over exactly that fraction.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter 6

quotations.text: White Fang was bitter and implacable. The clay of him was so moulded. He declared a vendetta against all dogs.
quotations.context: White Fang as lead dog, hated by the team, in the chapter called The Enemy of His Kind.
quotations.analysis: The clay sentence is placed between a description of temper and a declaration of war, as if it explained both, and it is the first appearance of a phrase the book will repeat for two men. 'Vendetta' is a human and legal word for a dog's behaviour; the mock-formality is how London keeps the reader from simply pitying him.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 1

quotations.text: In short, Beauty Smith was a monstrosity, and the blame of it lay elsewhere. He was not responsible. The clay of him had been so moulded in the making.
quotations.context: The narrator introduces the cook at Fort Yukon who wants to buy White Fang.
quotations.analysis: The same sentence that explained the wolf's ferocity is now applied to the man who will torment him, and it removes his responsibility in three words. Readers who accept the argument for the animal are being asked whether they will accept it for the villain; the book does not soften Smith in the least, and still insists he did not make himself.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 2

quotations.text: For Beauty Smith was cruel in the way that cowards are cruel. Cringing and snivelling himself before the blows or angry speech of a man, he revenged himself, in turn, upon creatures weaker than he. All life likes power, and Beauty Smith was no exception.
quotations.context: Beauty Smith beats White Fang after buying him from Grey Beaver.
quotations.analysis: Cruelty is explained as a hydraulic system: pressure applied from above is passed downward to whatever is weaker. The generalisation 'all life likes power' includes the wolf, who has been enjoying his vendetta against dogs for a whole chapter, and it declines to make Smith a different order of being from the animal he is beating.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 2

quotations.text: Under the tutelage of the mad god, White Fang became a fiend. He was kept chained in a pen at the rear of the fort, and here Beauty Smith teased and irritated and drove him wild with petty torments.
quotations.context: The opening of the chapter called The Reign of Hate.
quotations.analysis: 'Tutelage' is a schoolroom word, and it keeps the book's insistence that ferocity is taught. The mad god is the third god White Fang has known and the first who is insane by the standards of the others, so that the theology built up in Part III now has a devil in it. 'Petty' is the exact word: the damage is done by small things, repeated.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 3

quotations.text: Nevertheless, Nature had given him plasticity. Where many another animal would have died or had its spirit broken, he adjusted himself and lived, and at no expense of the spirit.
quotations.context: White Fang is exhibited in a cage as the Fighting Wolf and fought against dogs.
quotations.analysis: Plasticity is the property that makes the clay metaphor work, and here it is credited to Nature rather than to any master — the one gift that is his by birth is the capacity to be changed. The sentence also plants the possibility of the last two parts: an animal that can be moulded into a fiend can, at cost, be moulded back.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 3

quotations.text: Weedon Scott had set himself the task of redeeming White Fang⁠—or rather, of redeeming mankind from the wrong it had done White Fang. It was a matter of principle and conscience. He felt that the ill done White Fang was a debt incurred by man and that it must be paid.
quotations.context: Scott begins the slow work of taming the wolf he has bought out of the ring.
quotations.analysis: The correction after the dash reverses who is being redeemed. Scott is not rescuing a dog; he is settling an account on behalf of his species, and the vocabulary — debt, incurred, paid — is that of a ledger rather than a sermon. It matters that the motive is principle, not affection: love, in this book, is what comes afterwards.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 6

quotations.text: The thumb of circumstance had done its work only too well. By it he had been formed and hardened into the Fighting Wolf, fierce and implacable, unloving and unlovable.
quotations.context: The narrator weighs what Scott is up against.
quotations.analysis: The potter's thumb is the clay figure completed: circumstance has hands. The final pair of adjectives is a small structure in itself, cause and effect in two words that differ by a syllable, and the sentence that follows in the text describes the reversal Scott is attempting as a reflux of being — the book's admission that its own thesis makes redemption almost impossible.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 6

quotations.text: He had gone to the roots of White Fang’s nature, and with kindness touched to life potencies that had languished and well-nigh perished. One such potency was love.
quotations.context: The turning point of the novel, in the chapter called The Love-Master.
quotations.analysis: Love is introduced as a dormant capacity, something that was always in the clay and nearly died of disuse, which keeps it inside the book's materialism: it is not a miracle but a revival. After three hundred pages in which the word has appeared only to say that he did not know it, the two-word predicate 'was love' lands with the weight of a whole part.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 6

quotations.text: Having learned to snuggle, White Fang was guilty of it often. It was the final word. He could not go beyond it.
quotations.context: After Scott's return from a journey during which White Fang refused to eat.
quotations.analysis: 'Guilty' is the joke and the point: a fighting wolf caught in an act of tenderness, described in the language of an offence. The narrator then treats snuggling as speech — a final word — for a creature the book has repeatedly reminded us cannot talk, so that the most articulate thing he does in five parts is put his head under a man's arm.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter 6

quotations.text: He knew the law even better than did the dogs that had known no other life, and he observed the law more punctiliously; but still there was about him a suggestion of lurking ferocity, as though the Wild still lingered in him and the wolf in him merely slept.
quotations.context: White Fang settled at Sierra Vista, obeying the household's rules.
quotations.analysis: The sentence balances on its semicolon: obedience on one side, ferocity on the other, and 'merely' doing more work than it seems. The last chapter is called The Sleeping Wolf, and this is where the title is prepared — the tamed animal is presented as a sleeper who could wake, which the plot then requires him to do on a staircase.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part V, Chapter 4

quotations.text: And outside he went, like a king, with all Sierra Vista about him and tending on him. He was very weak, and when he reached the lawn he lay down and rested for a while.
quotations.context: White Fang, recovered from three bullets and a broken leg, is let out into the sun.
quotations.analysis: The king's progress lasts one sentence and then he has to lie down. It is the book's habit to grant a grand image and immediately correct it with a physical fact, and here the correction is tender rather than mocking. The wolf who once had a crowd around a cage now has a household around a lawn — the same shape, inverted.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part V, Chapter 5

quotations.text: The other puppies came sprawling toward him, to Collie’s great disgust; and he gravely permitted them to clamber and tumble over him.
quotations.context: The last paragraph of the novel.
quotations.analysis: 'Gravely permitted' is the whole character in two words — the outcast who never played, now allowing himself to be played on, with the dignity of a creature who has no idea how to do it. The novel ends with the animal that was moulded by hurt being climbed over by his own young, and London leaves the moral to the verb.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part V, Chapter 5

timeline.label: Jack London born in San Francisco
timeline.detail: Born John Griffith Chaney; he took the surname of his stepfather, John London.

timeline.label: Gold found on a tributary of the Klondike
timeline.detail: The strike that sent thousands up the Yukon to Dawson in the summers that followed — the traffic Grey Beaver trades with at Fort Yukon.

timeline.label: London goes north to the Klondike
timeline.detail: He wintered in the Yukon and came out the next year with scurvy and the material for a decade of Northland fiction.

timeline.label: The summer in which Part IV is set
timeline.detail: The novel dates White Fang's arrival at Fort Yukon to the summer of 1898, the height of the rush to Dawson.

timeline.label: The Call of the Wild published
timeline.detail: London's first Northland novel, whose journey from house to wild this book was planned to reverse.

timeline.label: The nature-faker dispute begins
timeline.detail: John Burroughs attacks sentimental animal writers in the Atlantic Monthly, opening the argument about what animals can be said to think.

timeline.label: White Fang serialised in Outing
timeline.detail: Six monthly instalments from May to October, with the Macmillan book following in October.

timeline.label: Theodore Roosevelt joins the nature-faker controversy
timeline.detail: The President's published criticism of animal writers singled out the fight between a wolf-dog and a bulldog.

timeline.label: London replies with The Other Animals
timeline.detail: Published in Collier's in September, defending the reasoning he had given his dogs.

timeline.label: Jack London dies at Glen Ellen
timeline.detail: Aged forty, on the ranch in the Sonoma Valley where he had written the novel.

timeline.label: Disney's White Fang
timeline.detail: The best-known screen version keeps the Klondike and Beauty Smith and adds a human boy for the wolf to belong to.

places.name: Mackenzie River, Northwest Territories
places.note: The frozen waterway of Part I, the river beside which the she-wolf litters, and the country of Grey Beaver's people.

places.name: Great Slave Lake
places.note: Kiche is traded away on a journey up the Mackenzie to the lake, and it is in a village there that White Fang first bites a man and learns the gods' law.

places.name: Fort Yukon, Alaska
places.note: The old Hudson's Bay Company post just under the Arctic circle, where Grey Beaver trades in the summer of 1898 and sells White Fang for whisky.

places.name: Dawson City, Yukon
places.note: Beauty Smith takes the Fighting Wolf up the Yukon by steamboat to the gold-rush town, where the bulldog Cherokee is waiting.

places.name: San Francisco
places.note: The slimy pavement and towering buildings of White Fang's first city, and the slum in which the convict Jim Hall was made.

places.name: Santa Clara Valley, California
places.note: Judge Scott's estate, Sierra Vista, where the last part is set — the same Southland valley from which London had taken Buck.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes London at his word: the book demonstrates that character is made by environment, and the repeated figure of clay and the moulding hand is its method as well as its message. On this view the narrator's generalisations are not intrusions but the point.
criticalViews.counter: A thesis that explains the villain and the hero equally well explains nothing about why one animal is redeemed and not another; the novel's turn to love in Part IV is a change of kind, not of pressure.

criticalViews.position: The Call of the Wild reversed, and the weaker for it
criticalViews.summary: Many readers have found the earlier book the stronger because its direction — towards the wild — is the one London's prose believes in. White Fang, running the other way, has to make domestication a happy ending, and some critics find the Southland chapters sentimental where the Northland ones are hard.
criticalViews.counter: The Southland is not written as paradise: it is a place of more laws, more gods and a cuff that hurts worse than a club, and the book's last word on the wolf is that he merely sleeps.

criticalViews.summary: The nature-faker controversy, in which Roosevelt criticised London's fighting scene, made the novel evidence in a public dispute about whether animals reason. London's careful hedging — he did not think the law, he lived it — reads as a working answer to that question, and one that later writers on animal cognition have found less naive than its critics did.
criticalViews.counter: The same hedging can be read as having it both ways: the narrator grants the wolf a full inner life and then denies him the words for it whenever the plausibility runs out.

essayQuestions.question: 'The clay of him was so moulded.' How far does White Fang persuade you that character is made by environment?
essayQuestions.focus: The nature-and-nurture thesis and its limits
plan: Set out the figure of clay as it is used for White Fang in Part IV, Chapter 1, and note that the same words are applied to Beauty Smith and to Jim Hall.
Trace the pressures the book itself names — Lip-lip, the club, the cage and the laughter — and show how each is credited with a specific change in temper.
Turn to what is credited to Nature alone: plasticity, and the fierceness that made the grey cub the one survivor of the litter.
Test the thesis against Part IV, Chapter 6, where redemption is described as a reflux of being achieved after the clay has hardened.
Conclude with the last chapter: whether the sleeping wolf who wakes on the stairs proves the thesis or admits its limit.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of the three masters — Grey Beaver, Beauty Smith and Weedon Scott.
essayQuestions.focus: Foils, gods and the meaning of service
plan: Establish the theology of Part III: what makes a man-animal a god, and what a god may do that a dog may not.
Read Grey Beaver as justice without affection, using the sale of Kiche and the naming speech, and note the narrator's remark about the plummet of affection he lacked.
Examine Beauty Smith as the mad god, and the narrator's insistence that he too was moulded and is not responsible.
Consider Scott's project as a debt to be paid rather than a rescue, and the moments where the book counts its cost to him.
Weigh whether the sequence is a controlled experiment or a moral ladder, and what the Southland's many gods add to the pattern.

essayQuestions.question: How does London write an animal's mind without making it human?
essayQuestions.focus: Animal focalisation and the narrator's interventions
plan: Begin in the lair: the wall of light, the classification of things that hurt, and the refusal to give the cub concepts before he has experiences.
Show the narrator's habit of stating a law and then withdrawing it from the animal — he did not think the law, he merely lived it.
Analyse the elevated diction (Mars, generalisations, adamantine texture) as a deliberate gap between the telling and the thing told.
Set this against the nature-faker controversy and Roosevelt's objection to the fight with Cherokee.
Decide whether the method holds in Part V, where snuggling becomes a final word and love a potency, or whether the animal has quietly become a person.

essayQuestions.question: 'A prologue about wolves, and then a book about men.' Is Part I necessary?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, the Wild and the human frame
plan: Describe what Part I establishes before the cub exists: the Wild as antagonist, the pack as a hunger, the she-wolf's dog trick.
Show how the coffin and the talk of epitaphs set the price of life in the North for men and dogs alike.
Trace the she-wolf from Part I into Part II and III, where she becomes Kiche, and argue what is gained by meeting her first as a predator.
Consider the symmetry with Part V, where the book again spends its attention on human beings — a judge, a convict, a household.
Conclude on whether the human frame makes the animal's story legible or simply dilutes it.

discussionQuestions: The narrator says Beauty Smith 'was not responsible' for his cruelty. Does the book mean it, and does it extend the same excuse to White Fang?
White Fang comes back to Grey Beaver's fire of his own accord after one night in the Wild. Is that a choice, and what would the book lose if it were forced?
Love is described as a 'potency' that had 'well-nigh perished'. Is London's account of love materialist, sentimental, or both at once?
Collie is allowed to bully White Fang for a season because she is female and he is forbidden to retaliate. What is the book saying about the laws of a house as opposed to the laws of the Wild?
The last chapter is called The Sleeping Wolf. After the killing of Jim Hall, is the wolf asleep, awake, or something the book cannot decide?

related.why: The book this one was written to reverse: a Californian dog going north into the wild, three years earlier and half the length.
The same American naturalism applied to a boy under fire, with instinct and fear examined as coolly as London examines a wolf.
Published two years later and the opposite method: animals given houses, manners and speech rather than hunger and clay.
Crane's men in an indifferent sea, where survival is again a matter of conditions rather than deserving.
An earlier and more famous argument that a creature is made monstrous by how it is treated, told from the creature's side.
